claim: Cancer immunotherapy by immune checkpoint blockade has saved the lives of a proportion of late stage patients with immunogenic tumor types.
source: Cancer immunotherapy by immune checkpoint blockade has proven its great potential by saving the lives of a proportion of late stage patients with immunogenic tumor types.
evidence: This is a general statement about the clinical success of immune checkpoint blockade therapy, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: The majority of patients with immunogenic tumor types do not sufficiently respond to immune checkpoint blockade therapy.
source: However, even in these sensitive tumor types, the majority of patients do not sufficiently respond to the therapy.
evidence: This statement reflects established clinical observations about the limitations of checkpoint blockade therapy.

claim: Glioblastoma remains largely refractory to immune checkpoint blockade therapy.
source: Furthermore, other tumor types, including glioblastoma, remain largely refractory.
evidence: This is a statement about the clinical response of glioblastoma to checkpoint blockade, representing established knowledge.

claim: The glioblastoma immune microenvironment is highly immunosuppressive.
source: The glioblastoma immune microenvironment is recognized as highly immunosuppressive, posing a major hurdle for inducing immune-mediated destruction of cancer cells.
evidence: This is a characterization of the glioblastoma immune microenvironment based on established research.

claim: Glioblastoma tumors contain tumor-associated macrophages, tumor-infiltrating dendritic cells and regulatory T cells.
source: Scattered information is available about the presence and activity of immunosuppressive or immunostimulatory cell types in glioblastoma tumors, including tumor-associated macrophages, tumor-infiltrating dendritic cells and regulatory T cells.
evidence: This statement describes the composition of immune cells in glioblastoma tumors based on existing literature.

claim: Immune cell types in glioblastoma are heterogeneous at the level of ontogeny, spatial distribution and functionality.
source: These cell types are heterogeneous at the level of ontogeny, spatial distribution and functionality within the tumor immune compartment, providing insight in the complex cellular and molecular interplay that determines the immune refractory state in glioblastoma.
evidence: This statement characterizes the heterogeneity of immune cells in glioblastoma based on research findings.

claim: Immune checkpoint blockers are monoclonal antibodies that inhibit molecules involved in downregulating T-cell activation such as CTLA-4 or PD-1.
source: The main progress came from immune checkpoint blockers (ICB), monoclonal antibodies that inhibit the function of molecules involved in downregulating T-cell activation such as CTLA-4 or PD-1.
evidence: This is a definition of immune checkpoint blockers based on established knowledge.

claim: ICB has shown the potential of curing late stage metastatic patients with highly immunogenic tumors such as melanoma, Merkel cell carcinoma or microsatellite instability (MSI)-high cancers.
source: ICB has shown the spectacular potential of curing late stage metastatic patients with highly immunogenic tumors such as melanoma, Merkel cell carcinoma or microsatellite instability (MSI)-high cancers, largely explaining its success.
evidence: This statement describes clinical outcomes of ICB therapy in specific tumor types, representing established knowledge.

claim: The majority of melanoma patients do not benefit from ICB.
source: However, the majority of patients, even in responsive tumor types such as melanoma, do not benefit from ICB.
evidence: This is a statement about clinical response rates in melanoma, representing established knowledge.

claim: Glioblastoma is the highest-grade, most prevalent and most aggressive glial tumor.
source: Glioblastoma (GBM), the highest-grade, most prevalent and most aggressive glial tumor, is one of the cancers in which ICB has met little success so far.
evidence: This is a characterization of glioblastoma based on established medical knowledge.

claim: ICB has met little success in glioblastoma.
source: Glioblastoma (GBM), the highest-grade, most prevalent and most aggressive glial tumor, is one of the cancers in which ICB has met little success so far.
evidence: This statement reflects clinical trial outcomes for ICB in glioblastoma.

claim: The inherently heterogenous nature of glioblastoma within individuals could be responsible for ICB failure.
source: Several underlying mechanisms could be responsible for this failure, including the inherently heterogenous nature of this tumor type within individuals and the establishment of an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about mechanisms of ICB resistance based on inference from tumor characteristics.

claim: The establishment of an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment could be responsible for ICB failure in glioblastoma.
source: Several underlying mechanisms could be responsible for this failure, including the inherently heterogenous nature of this tumor type within individuals and the establishment of an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about mechanisms of ICB resistance based on inference from tumor characteristics.

claim: Growth of GBM tumors is mediated by stem-like cells.
source: Growth of GBM tumors, but also resistance to radiotherapy and chemotherapies, is mediated by stem-like cells, whose tumor-propagating nature is fully regulated by a core set of neurodevelopmental transcription factors such as POU3F2, SOX2, SALL2, and OLIG2 (Suvà et al., 2014) (Figure 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Suvà et al., 2014.

claim: Resistance to radiotherapy and chemotherapies in GBM is mediated by stem-like cells.
source: Growth of GBM tumors, but also resistance to radiotherapy and chemotherapies, is mediated by stem-like cells, whose tumor-propagating nature is fully regulated by a core set of neurodevelopmental transcription factors such as POU3F2, SOX2, SALL2, and OLIG2 (Suvà et al., 2014) (Figure 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Suvà et al., 2014.

claim: The tumor-propagating nature of GBM stem-like cells is fully regulated by a core set of neurodevelopmental transcription factors such as POU3F2, SOX2, SALL2, and OLIG2.
source: Growth of GBM tumors, but also resistance to radiotherapy and chemotherapies, is mediated by stem-like cells, whose tumor-propagating nature is fully regulated by a core set of neurodevelopmental transcription factors such as POU3F2, SOX2, SALL2, and OLIG2 (Suvà et al., 2014) (Figure 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Suvà et al., 2014 and reference to Figure 1.

claim: Various markers have been suggested for glioblastoma stem cells.
source: Various markers have been suggested for glioblastoma stem cells (Lathia et al., 2015), but it is unclear at present whether different subpopulations of GBM stem cells exist and whether these give rise to tumors with a different cellular composition.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lathia et al., 2015.

claim: It is unclear whether different subpopulations of GBM stem cells exist.
source: Various markers have been suggested for glioblastoma stem cells (Lathia et al., 2015), but it is unclear at present whether different subpopulations of GBM stem cells exist and whether these give rise to tumors with a different cellular composition.
evidence: This statement acknowledges a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Expression profiling of GBM tumors identified at least three GBM subtypes: proneural (TCGA-PN), classical (TCGA-CL) and mesenchymal (TCGA-MES).
source: In any case, expression profiling of GBM tumors identified at least three GBM subtypes: proneural (TCGA-PN), classical (TCGA-CL) and mesenchymal (TCGA-MES) (Verhaak et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2017), which tend to differentially associate with abnormalities in PDGFRA, IDH1, EGFR and NF1 (Verhaak et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Verhaak et al., 2010 and Wang et al., 2017.

claim: GBM subtypes tend to differentially associate with abnormalities in PDGFRA, IDH1, EGFR and NF1.
source: In any case, expression profiling of GBM tumors identified at least three GBM subtypes: proneural (TCGA-PN), classical (TCGA-CL) and mesenchymal (TCGA-MES) (Verhaak et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2017), which tend to differentially associate with abnormalities in PDGFRA, IDH1, EGFR and NF1 (Verhaak et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Verhaak et al., 2010.

claim: Different GBM subtypes can be found within the same tumor.
source: This level of heterogeneity is dramatically increased by the notion that different GBM subtypes can be found within the same tumor and are dynamic in function of time or in response to therapy (Sottoriva et al., 2013; Patel et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sottoriva et al., 2013; Patel et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2017.

claim: GBM subtypes are dynamic in function of time or in response to therapy.
source: This level of heterogeneity is dramatically increased by the notion that different GBM subtypes can be found within the same tumor and are dynamic in function of time or in response to therapy (Sottoriva et al., 2013; Patel et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sottoriva et al., 2013; Patel et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2017.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing identified four cellular states for glioblastoma cells: mesenchymal-like (MES-like), astrocyte-like (AC-like), oligodendrocytic precursor cell-like (OPC-like) and neural progenitor cell-like (NPC-like).
source: More recent high-resolution single-cell RNA sequencing provided even more granularity to the concept of intra-tumoral heterogeneity by identifying four cellular states for glioblastoma cells: mesenchymal-like (MES-like), astrocyte-like (AC-like), oligodendrocytic precursor cell-like (OPC-like) and neural progenitor cell-like (NPC-like) (Neftel et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Neftel et al., 2019.

claim: TCGA-CL tumors are enriched in AC-like states.
source: There is a preponderance of particular states in each TCGA tumor type, with TCGA-CL and TCGA-MES being enriched in AC-like and MES-like states, respectively, and TCGA-PN encompassing both OPC-like and NPC-like states.
evidence: This statement describes the relationship between TCGA subtypes and cellular states, inferred from Neftel et al., 2019.

claim: TCGA-MES tumors are enriched in MES-like states.
source: There is a preponderance of particular states in each TCGA tumor type, with TCGA-CL and TCGA-MES being enriched in AC-like and MES-like states, respectively, and TCGA-PN encompassing both OPC-like and NPC-like states.
evidence: This statement describes the relationship between TCGA subtypes and cellular states, inferred from Neftel et al., 2019.

claim: TCGA-PN tumors encompass both OPC-like and NPC-like states.
source: There is a preponderance of particular states in each TCGA tumor type, with TCGA-CL and TCGA-MES being enriched in AC-like and MES-like states, respectively, and TCGA-PN encompassing both OPC-like and NPC-like states.
evidence: This statement describes the relationship between TCGA subtypes and cellular states, inferred from Neftel et al., 2019.

claim: Some genetic alterations favor specific cellular states, with EGFR overexpression driving an AC-like program.
source: Notably, some genetic alterations favor specific cellular states, with for example EGFR overexpression driving an AC-like program (Neftel et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Neftel et al., 2019.

claim: Non-genetic heterogeneity within GBM tumors is determined by the relative proximity of cancer cells to blood vessels.
source: Finally, non-genetic heterogeneity within GBM tumors is determined by the relative proximity of cancer cells to blood vessels, with mTOR activity being upregulated in the few cell layers closest to the vessels (Kumar et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kumar et al., 2019.

claim: mTOR activity is upregulated in the few cell layers closest to blood vessels in GBM tumors.
source: Finally, non-genetic heterogeneity within GBM tumors is determined by the relative proximity of cancer cells to blood vessels, with mTOR activity being upregulated in the few cell layers closest to the vessels (Kumar et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kumar et al., 2019.

claim: In GBM cells close to blood vessels, mTOR conveys superior invasive and migratory capabilities and resistance to therapy.
source: In these cells, mTOR conveys superior invasive and migratory capabilities and resistance to therapy.
evidence: This statement is inferred from the Kumar et al., 2019 study mentioned in the previous sentence.

claim: The highly heterogeneous nature of GBM strongly undermines the efficacy of therapy.
source: Together, this highly heterogeneous nature of GBM strongly undermines the efficacy of therapy, considering the likely presence of cancer cell clones which are able to escape.
evidence: This is an inference based on the described heterogeneity and the concept of clonal escape.

claim: Defects in anti-tumor T-cell responses are commonly observed in GBM.
source: In addition, defects in anti-tumor T-cell responses are commonly observed in GBM, suggesting the active induction of immunosuppression.
evidence: This statement represents established knowledge about T-cell dysfunction in GBM.

claim: Intracranial tumors cause an entrapment of T cells in the bone marrow due to a loss of surface spingosine-1-phosphate receptor 1 (S1P1).
source: In this respect, intracranial tumors of various histological origins (not only GBM) cause an entrapment of T cells in the bone marrow due to a loss of surface spingosine-1-phosphate receptor 1 (S1P1) (Chongsathidkiet et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chongsathidkiet et al., 2018.

claim: A reversal of S1P1 deficiency enables an enhanced migration of T cells into GBM tumors.
source: Why only intracranial tumors induce this defect and via which mechanism is currently unknown, but a reversal of this deficiency enables an enhanced migration of T cells into GBM tumors.
evidence: This statement is inferred from the Chongsathidkiet et al., 2018 study mentioned in the previous sentence.

claim: Thymic involution in GBM tumor-bearers results in diminished T-cell production.
source: Along the same line, thymic involution in GBM tumor-bearers results in diminished T-cell production and, hence, reduced availability of T cells for anti-GBM immunity (Andaloussi et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Andaloussi et al., 2008.

claim: Thymic involution in GBM tumor-bearers results in reduced availability of T cells for anti-GBM immunity.
source: Along the same line, thymic involution in GBM tumor-bearers results in diminished T-cell production and, hence, reduced availability of T cells for anti-GBM immunity (Andaloussi et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Andaloussi et al., 2008.

claim: T cells inside GBM tumors are likely to become dysfunctional via various mechanisms.
source: Moreover, once T cells do get inside the GBM tumor, they are likely to become dysfunctional via various mechanisms (Woroniecka et al., 2018a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Woroniecka et al., 2018a.

claim: Exhausted T cells are enriched within GBM tumors.
source: Recent studies provide evidence for the enriched presence of exhausted T cells within GBM tumors, with tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) more often co-expressing the immune checkpoint molecules PD-1, LAG3 and TIM-3 than peripheral blood cells of patients or healthy controls (Woroniecka et al., 2018b; Davidson et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Woroniecka et al., 2018b and Davidson et al., 2019.

claim: Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes in GBM more often co-express PD-1, LAG3 and TIM-3 than peripheral blood cells of patients or healthy controls.
source: Recent studies provide evidence for the enriched presence of exhausted T cells within GBM tumors, with tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) more often co-expressing the immune checkpoint molecules PD-1, LAG3 and TIM-3 than peripheral blood cells of patients or healthy controls (Woroniecka et al., 2018b; Davidson et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Woroniecka et al., 2018b and Davidson et al., 2019.

claim: PD-1+ LAG3+ TIM-3+ T cells showed impaired T-cell functions.
source: Interestingly, PD-1+ LAG3+ TIM-3+ T cells showed impaired T-cell functions, while single positive cells for any of these markers did not.
evidence: This statement is inferred from the studies mentioned in the previous sentence (Woroniecka et al., 2018b; Davidson et al., 2019).

claim: Single positive cells for PD-1, LAG3, or TIM-3 did not show impaired T-cell functions.
source: Interestingly, PD-1+ LAG3+ TIM-3+ T cells showed impaired T-cell functions, while single positive cells for any of these markers did not.
evidence: This statement is inferred from the studies mentioned in the previous sentence (Woroniecka et al., 2018b; Davidson et al., 2019).

claim: T-cell dysfunctionality in GBM is mediated by the presence of suppressive cells such as regulatory T cells (Treg) and tumor-associated macrophages (TAM).
source: A second prominent mechanism of T-cell dysfunctionality is tolerance, mediated by the presence of suppressive cells such as regulatory T cells (Treg) and tumor-associated macrophages (TAM).
evidence: This statement represents established knowledge about mechanisms of T-cell suppression in tumors.

claim: Preclinical models have provided a proof-of-concept that ICB with anti-CTLA-4 and/or anti-PD-1 improves tumor outcome in GBM.
source: In summary, preclinical models have provided a proof-of-concept that ICB with anti-CTLA-4 and/or anti-PD-1, either as monotherapy or in conjunction with standard-of-care treatments, improves tumor outcome.
evidence: This statement summarizes findings from preclinical studies as referenced in previous reviews (Romani et al., 2018; Simonelli et al., 2018).

claim: The timing of ICB administration could majorly impact its effect.
source: One of the most noticeable advances comes from the realization that the timing of ICB administration could majorly impact its effect.
evidence: This statement is based on inference from recent clinical and preclinical findings discussed in the following text.

claim: Neoadjuvant therapy has proven to be advantageous in breast, bladder and other types of cancer.
source: Neoadjuvant (pre-operative) therapy has proven to be advantageous in breast, bladder and other types of cancer, but this finding remained restricted to chemo- and radiation therapy with very little data available on ICB neoadjuvant therapy until recently (O'Donnell et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to O'Donnell et al., 2019.

claim: Neoadjuvant immunotherapy increased anti-tumor immune responses and survival in two mouse models of triple-negative breast cancer.
source: Liu et al. (2016) demonstrated increased anti-tumor immune responses and survival upon neoadjuvant immunotherapy, in two mouse models of triple-negative breast cancer.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2016.

claim: Neoadjuvant immunotherapy has been reproduced in several preclinical models.
source: This finding has now been reproduced in several other preclinical models (O'Donnell et al., 2019), and importantly, also in the clinical setting of resectable melanoma (Blank et al., 2018; Amaria et al., 2018; Rozeman et al., 2019) and glioblastoma (Cloughesy et al., 2019; Schalper et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to O'Donnell et al., 2019.

claim: Neoadjuvant immunotherapy has shown efficacy in the clinical setting of resectable melanoma.
source: This finding has now been reproduced in several other preclinical models (O'Donnell et al., 2019), and importantly, also in the clinical setting of resectable melanoma (Blank et al., 2018; Amaria et al., 2018; Rozeman et al., 2019) and glioblastoma (Cloughesy et al., 2019; Schalper et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Blank et al., 2018; Amaria et al., 2018; Rozeman et al., 2019.

claim: Neoadjuvant immunotherapy has shown efficacy in the clinical setting of glioblastoma.
source: This finding has now been reproduced in several other preclinical models (O'Donnell et al., 2019), and importantly, also in the clinical setting of resectable melanoma (Blank et al., 2018; Amaria et al., 2018; Rozeman et al., 2019) and glioblastoma (Cloughesy et al., 2019; Schalper et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cloughesy et al., 2019; Schalper et al., 2019.

claim: In resectable glioblastoma, one neoadjuvant injection of anti-PD-1 followed by surgical resection and repeated adjuvant anti-PD-1 treatment resulted in a significant increase in overall survival and progression-free survival compared to adjuvant treatment alone.
source: In resectable glioblastoma, either as primary or recurrent tumor, one neoadjuvant injection of anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibodies, followed by surgical resection of the tumor and repeated adjuvant anti-PD-1 treatment, resulted in a significant increase in overall survival and progression-free survival compared to adjuvant treatment alone (Cloughesy et al., 2019; Schalper et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cloughesy et al., 2019; Schalper et al., 2019.

claim: Neoadjuvant anti-PD-1 treatment resulted in an intratumoral immunomodulatory effect, with an increased interferon response, production of chemokines, and signs of increased TIL activity.
source: Both studies also demonstrated an intratumoral immunomodulatory effect of the neoadjuvant treatment, with an increased interferon response, production of chemokines, and signs of increased TIL activity.
evidence: This statement is inferred from the studies by Cloughesy et al., 2019 and Schalper et al., 2019 mentioned in the previous sentences.

claim: Anti-PD-1 efficacy is boosted by concurrent administration of chemotherapy in preclinical models.
source: A second level of innovation comes from the assessment of novel combination therapies in preclinical models, whereby anti-PD-1 efficacy is boosted by a concurrent administration of chemotherapy (Park et al., 2019), radiation therapy (Rajani et al., 2018), other immune checkpoint blocking monoclonal antibodies (Wu et al., 2019), cancer cell-directed immunotoxins (Chandramohan et al., 2019), and nanocarriers that improve the shuttling of ICB across the blood-brain barrier (Galstyan et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Park et al., 2019.

claim: Anti-PD-1 efficacy is boosted by concurrent administration of radiation therapy in preclinical models.
source: A second level of innovation comes from the assessment of novel combination therapies in preclinical models, whereby anti-PD-1 efficacy is boosted by a concurrent administration of chemotherapy (Park et al., 2019), radiation therapy (Rajani et al., 2018), other immune checkpoint blocking monoclonal antibodies (Wu et al., 2019), cancer cell-directed immunotoxins (Chandramohan et al., 2019), and nanocarriers that improve the shuttling of ICB across the blood-brain barrier (Galstyan et al., 2019).

evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Galstyan et al., 2019.

claim: Monotherapies usually have little impact on GBM, highlighting the strongly immunosuppressive nature of the GBM tumor microenvironment.
source: Indeed, monotherapies usually have little impact, highlighting the strongly immunosuppressive nature of the GBM tumor microenvironment (TME).
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the described combination therapy studies and established knowledge about GBM.

claim: Oncolytic viruses cause a direct killing of highly proliferative cancer cells.
source: A novel avenue to increase the immunogenicity of the GBM TME comes from virotherapy, whereby oncolytic viruses not only cause a direct killing of highly proliferative cancer cells but also trigger an (innate) immune response (Iorgulescu et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Iorgulescu et al., 2018.

claim: Oncolytic viruses trigger an (innate) immune response.
source: A novel avenue to increase the immunogenicity of the GBM TME comes from virotherapy, whereby oncolytic viruses not only cause a direct killing of highly proliferative cancer cells but also trigger an (innate) immune response (Iorgulescu et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Iorgulescu et al., 2018.

claim: Intratumoral injections of a polio-rhinovirus chimera achieved a 21% rate of longer term survivors (at least 2 to 3 years) in a clinical trial.
source: For example, a recent clinical trial applied intratumoral injections of a polio-rhinovirus chimera and could achieve a remarkable 21% of longer term survivors (at least 2 to 3 years), while <4% of such patients is observed in control groups (Desjardins et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Desjardins et al., 2018.

claim: In a phase I study with DNX-2401, 20% of patients survived >3 years from treatment.
source: In a phase I study with DNX-2401, a tumor-selective replication-competent oncolytic adenovirus, 20% of patients survived >3 years from treatment, and three patients had a ≥ 95% reduction of the tumor, which was probably due to direct oncolytic effects of the virus followed by elicitation of an immune-mediated antiglioma response (Lang et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lang et al., 2018.

claim: In a phase I study with DNX-2401, three patients had a ≥ 95% reduction of the tumor.
source: In a phase I study with DNX-2401, a tumor-selective replication-competent oncolytic adenovirus, 20% of patients survived >3 years from treatment, and three patients had a ≥ 95% reduction of the tumor, which was probably due to direct oncolytic effects of the virus followed by elicitation of an immune-mediated antiglioma response (Lang et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lang et al., 2018.

claim: The tumor reduction in DNX-2401 treated patients was probably due to direct oncolytic effects of the virus followed by elicitation of an immune-mediated antiglioma response.

evidence: This statement is an inference from the Lang et al., 2018 study.

claim: Novel generations of CAR T-cells are being generated that should show improved functionality in the TME from GBM.
source: A passive transfer of anti-tumor T-effector cells could be an alternative strategy to attack GBM tumors, although such T cells should then be able to withstand the suppressive TME. Novel generations of CAR T-cells are being generated that should show improved functionality in the TME, including the TME from GBM (Petersen and Krenciute, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Petersen and Krenciute, 2019.

claim: DC vaccination has yielded some efficacy in improving the median overall survival in clinical trials.
source: Finally, the adoptive transfer of antigen-presenting dendritic cells (i.e. DC vaccination) has yielded some efficacy in improving the median overall survival in clinical trials (Srivastava et al., 2019) and further research is warranted to improve the treatment regimens and the choice of the most optimal DC type and the most optimal tumor antigens.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Srivastava et al., 2019.

claim: Neoantigens show efficacy as vaccine candidates in glioblastoma patients.
source: Neoantigens are the most tumor-specific and arguably the most promising antigen candidates, that show efficacy as vaccine candidates in glioblastoma patients (Keskin et al., 2019; Hilf et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Keskin et al., 2019 and Hilf et al., 2019.

claim: The immune contexture of human tumors changes at each tumor stage and has an impact on clinical outcome.
source: The immune contexture of human tumors, referring to the exact composition of distinct immune cell types within tumors, changes at each tumor stage and is known to have an impact on clinical outcome (Fridman et al., 2012; Bindea et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Fridman et al., 2012 and Bindea et al., 2013.

claim: Understanding the tumor immune microenvironment has been recognized as one of the future challenges to improve therapy of brain tumors.
source: Hence, understanding the tumor (immune) microenvironment has recently been recognized as one of the future challenges to improve therapy of brain tumors (Aldape et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Aldape et al., 2019.

claim: Glioblastoma tumors contain a dominance of immunosuppressive cells.
source: Glioblastoma tumors are known to contain a variety of immune cell types, but with a dominance of immunosuppressive cells.
evidence: This statement represents established knowledge about the GBM immune microenvironment.

claim: Distinct subpopulations exist within the immunoregulatory macrophage compartment of glioblastoma tumors.
source: Recent findings further finetune this concept through the identification of distinct subpopulations within the immunoregulatory macrophage compartment of tumors, but also distinct Treg and dendritic cell subsets have been identified and will be discussed in this review.
evidence: This statement is based on recent research findings that will be discussed in the review.

claim: Distinct Treg subsets have been identified in glioblastoma tumors.

evidence: This statement is based on recent research findings that will be discussed in the review.

claim: Distinct dendritic cell subsets have been identified in glioblastoma tumors.

claim: TILs are enriched in TCGA-MES glioblastomas.
source: TILs are enriched in TCGA-MES glioblastomas and strongly associated with mutations in NF1 and RB1.
evidence: This statement is inferred from the Rutledge et al., 2013 study mentioned in the following sentence.

claim: TILs are strongly associated with mutations in NF1 and RB1.
source: TILs are enriched in TCGA-MES glioblastomas and strongly associated with mutations in NF1 and RB1. Conversely, TILs are depleted in the TCGA-CL class, EGFR-amplified, and homozygous PTEN-deleted tumors and rare in histologies characterized by these alterations (Rutledge et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rutledge et al., 2013.

claim: TILs are depleted in the TCGA-CL class, EGFR-amplified, and homozygous PTEN-deleted tumors.
source: Conversely, TILs are depleted in the TCGA-CL class, EGFR-amplified, and homozygous PTEN-deleted tumors and rare in histologies characterized by these alterations (Rutledge et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rutledge et al., 2013.

claim: The IDH mutant status in glioblastoma tumors significantly associates with TIL infiltration.
source: In addition, the IDH mutant status in glioblastoma tumors significantly associates with TIL infiltration.
evidence: This statement is based on the studies mentioned in the following sentences.

claim: The IDH-wt status is associated with significantly higher TIL infiltration and PD-L1 expression.
source: The IDH-wt status is associated with significantly higher TIL infiltration and PD-L1 expression (Berghoff et al., 2017), while IDH mutations result in the opposite phenotype, that is a reduced IFNγ signature and reduced presence of CD8+ and CD4+ cells (Kohanbash et al., 2017; Luoto et al., 2018).
